kurals.tamil:
கண்தாம் கலுழ்வ தெவன்கொலோ தண்டாநோய்
தாம்காட்ட யாம்கண் டது.
kurals.transliteration:
Kandhaam kaluzhva thevan-koloa thandaanoi
thaamkaatta yaamkan dadhu.
kurals.meaning: This unending love-sickness came to me only because my eyes showed him to me; so why do those same eyes now weep and beg to see him?
kurals.elementary: Imagine you begged your friend to let you hold their puppy, and then you cried when it was time to give it back. Your friend might say, ‘But you were the one who wanted to hold it!’ The lady in this couplet scolds her own eyes the same way: they were the ones who looked at him first, so why are they crying now?
kurals.university: Chapter 118 continues the karpiyal (married love) sequence on separation, and its whole conceit is that the heroine turns on her own eyes: kaṇ (eye) plus vituppu (eager longing, impatience) plus aḻital (wasting away), i.e. the eyes are worn out by their own craving to see the absent husband. In the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar she speaks to her confidante (tōḻi), half-blaming, half-pitying the eyes as if they were separate persons. Kaluḻvatu (கலுழ்வது) is ‘weeping’, taṇṭā nōy (தண்டாநோய்) ‘the disease that does not abate’, and tām kāṭṭa yām kaṇṭatu ‘we saw it because they showed it’: the eyes are both cause and complainant. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar sharpen the irony by making the eyes weep to be shown him again, while Pope renders: ‘They showed me him, and then my endless pain / I saw: why then should weeping eyes complain?’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a strong wind sweeps away a boat on the water, even one of the roaming senses on which the mind focuses can carry away a man’s intelligence.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that a single sense, once the mind follows it, can drag the whole person off course.
hinduism.tie_back: The heroine’s complaint is exactly this: one sense, her eyes, carried her into a love-sickness she cannot now steer out of.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.67 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a genuine teaching on the senses leading the self astray, though the Gita counsels restraint while the Kural’s speaker only reproaches her eyes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus speaks of the eye as a member that can lead the whole person into ruin, and so may be treated as an offender.
christianity.tie_back: Like Jesus’ saying, the Kural treats the eye as a culprit separate from the self, the one that ‘caused’ the trouble.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the eye-as-offender motif matches, but the context is moral temptation rather than love for a spouse.

islam.quote_or_event: “The adultery of the eyes is the sight (to gaze at a forbidden thing), the adultery of the tongue is the talk, and the inner self wishes and desires…”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes how desire begins with the eyes’ looking, which the inner self then turns into longing.
islam.tie_back: The Kural makes the same chain of cause: the eyes looked first, and the heart’s unending longing followed.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com (excerpted); the eyes-first chain of desire matches, though the hadith concerns illicit looking while the Kural’s love is for her own husband.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The heart and the eyes are the ‘spies’ of the body — they act as its agents for sinning: the eye sees, the heart covets and the body commits the sin.”
judaism.explanation: Rashi, citing the Midrash, explains that the eyes are the body’s scouts: they go first, and the heart’s desire follows what they report.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine likewise names her eyes as the scouts that went ahead and led her heart into its present suffering.
judaism.source: Rashi on Numbers 15:39 (tr. M. Rosenbaum and A.M. Silbermann, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; the eyes-as-agents image is a close structural parallel, though Rashi’s concern is sin, not married love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The eye is aflame. Forms are aflame. Consciousness at the eye is aflame. Contact at the eye is aflame.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Fire Sermon the Buddha teaches that seeing, and everything that arises from the eye’s contact with forms, burns with passion and brings sorrow and lamentation.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine discovers the same thing in her own life: what began with the eye’s contact has become a fire of grief.
buddhism.source: Adittapariyaya Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35.28 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it locates suffering in the eye’s contact as the Kural does, though its remedy is disenchantment, not reunion.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who passionately hates (a colour), will at the same moment suffer pain. It is the fault of an undisciplined man that he is annoyed (by a colour); it is not the ‘colour’ itself that annoys him.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that suffering from what the eye perceives comes from one’s own undisciplined attachment or aversion, not from the object seen.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine likewise refuses to blame anyone outside herself: the fault lies with her own eyes, which looked and clung.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it shares the Kural’s placing of blame on one’s own sense faculty, though the Jain aim is dispassion while the Kural’s speaker still longs for her husband.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orpheus wins Eurydice back from the underworld on condition that he not look at her until they reach the upper air, but at the last moment, longing to see her, he turns his eyes and loses her for ever, and then weeps for her.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s telling, it is Orpheus’s own longing look that costs him the beloved he then mourns.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the eyes that looked out of love become the cause of the grief they then weep over.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; the eyes-as-cause motif fits, but Orpheus loses his wife through one look rather than falling in love by sight.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that the pleasure of the eye is the beginning of love: no one falls in love who has not first been delighted by the beloved’s appearance, though delight in looks alone is not yet love.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, sight is the starting point of erotic love, which then grows into longing for the beloved’s presence.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine traces her ‘unending disease’ to that same beginning: her eyes’ first delighted look.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; a clear match for love beginning in the eye, though Aristotle is analysing goodwill rather than lamenting.

kurals.tamil:
தெரிந்துணரா நோக்கிய உண்கண் பரிந்துணராப்
பைதல் உழப்பது எவன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Therindhunaraa noakkiya un-kan parindhunaraap
paidhal uzhappadhu evan.
kurals.meaning: My kohl-darkened eyes looked at him back then without weighing what would follow; why do they now suffer, without understanding that the sorrow is of their own making?
kurals.elementary: Think of someone who eats a whole bag of sweets without thinking, and then complains of a tummy ache as if it came from nowhere. The lady says her eyes did the same: they gazed at him without thinking ahead, and now they cry as if they don’t know why it hurts.
kurals.university: The couplet balances two negated verbs of knowing: terintu uṇarā nōkkiya, ‘looked without discerning and understanding’ (then), and parintu uṇarā, ‘not perceiving with sympathy’ or ‘not grasping’ (now). Uṇkaṇ (உண்கண்) is the conventional ‘eye fit to be eaten’, i.e. kohl-lined and lovely, and paital (பைதல்) is grief or affliction; uḻappatu evaṉ asks ‘why do they toil in it?’ Mu. Varadarasanar reads the second clause as the eyes failing to feel affection now; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as the eyes failing to recognise that they brought this on themselves and should bear it. Pope gives: ‘How glancing eyes, that rash unweeting looked that day, / With sorrow measureless are wasting now away!’ No textual variants were found between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna traces a chain that begins with merely dwelling on sense objects: from that contemplation arises attachment, from attachment desire, from desire anger, and so on down to the loss of discernment and ruin.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita teaches that unreflective attention to an object is the first link in a chain that ends in suffering.
hinduism.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes ‘looked without discerning’, and the whole chain of longing and pain followed from that first unweighed glance.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not re-checked word for word this session; the chain from looking to suffering matches, though the Gita addresses spiritual discipline rather than married love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat…”
christianity.explanation: In Eden, what is ‘pleasant to the eyes’ is taken without weighing the consequence, and sorrow follows.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes likewise acted on delight without foresight, and are now left with the grief that followed.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a strong pattern of unconsidered looking followed by sorrow, though Eden concerns disobedience, not love.

islam.quote_or_event: “Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts. That is purer for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an asks believers to restrain their gaze, recognising that unguarded looking leads the heart where it should not go.
islam.tie_back: The heroine wishes, in effect, that her eyes had been more guarded and discerning when they first looked.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; the restraint-of-the-gaze principle fits, but the verse concerns modesty in general, not regret within marriage.

judaism.quote_or_event: “…that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them; and that ye go not about after your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go astray.”
judaism.explanation: The fringes (tzitzit) are given so that Israel will not follow wherever the heart and eyes wander.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes did just that, going ‘after’ what they saw without considering where it led.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); the warning against following one’s eyes matches, though the verse is about covenant faithfulness, not marital love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seeing your eyes, my sensual delight grows all the more.” — to which the nun Subha replies: “you run blind after what is unreal.”
buddhism.explanation: A libertine stops the nun Subha and confesses he is captivated by her eyes; she answers that his vision is distorted and he chases a mirage.
buddhism.tie_back: The libertine’s undiscerning gaze is the Kural’s ‘looking without understanding’; the Kural’s heroine is now living with what such looking leads to.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org (two separate lines joined); a vivid scene of infatuation through the eyes, though here the gazer is a would-be seducer, not a devoted wife.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana compares the person ruled by what the eye sees to a moth that flies into the flame it is drawn to.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes flew toward their beloved like the moth, without discernment, and are now burnt by the absence that followed.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a close image of the undiscerning eye rushing to its own harm, framed as a monastic warning rather than a lover’s lament.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Narcissus falls in love with a reflection in a pool without understanding what he is seeing; Ovid’s narrator tells him that what he seeks is nowhere and that he is deceived by his own eyes.
greek_mythology.explanation: Narcissus’s eyes fasten on an image before his mind grasps what it is, and he wastes away from that undiscerning gaze.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Narcissus, the Kural’s eyes ‘looked without understanding’ and brought on a pining they cannot escape.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; strong on undiscerning sight, though Narcissus loves an illusion while the heroine loves a real husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hume argues that reason alone can never oppose a passion in directing the will, and that reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions.
philosophy.explanation: On Hume’s view, desires are not first weighed by reason; they move us, and reason only follows.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes illustrate Hume’s point: they acted on delight, not on reflection, and reason arrives only afterwards to complain.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 2.3.3 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage, not checked word for word this session; it explains why the eyes looked without discerning, but Hume is making a general claim about motivation, not about love.

kurals.tamil:
கதுமெனத் தாநோக்கித் தாமே கலுழும்
இதுநகத் தக்க துடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Kadhumenath thaanoakkith thaamae kaluzhum
ithunakath thakka thudaiththu.
kurals.meaning: These eyes rushed of their own accord to look at him, and now of their own accord they weep; surely that deserves to be laughed at.
kurals.elementary: Picture a child who runs to jump in a puddle, then cries because their socks are wet. It’s sad, but also a little funny, because they did it to themselves! The lady laughs at her eyes the same way: they hurried to look, and now they are the ones crying.
kurals.university: Katumeṉa (கதுமென) is an adverb of sudden speed, ‘in a flash’, and the parallel tām (themselves) / tāmē (they themselves) puts the whole action, the eager looking and the weeping, on the eyes alone. Naka-t-takkatu uṭaittu, ‘it has the quality of something to be laughed at’, gives the chapter its bitter humour: the heroine mocks her own organs. Puliyur Kesikan glosses the laughter as at the eyes’ ignorance; Solomon Pappaiah renders it colloquially, ‘when I see these eyes crying alone today, I can only laugh’. Pope: ‘The eyes that threw such eager glances round erewhile / Are weeping now. Such folly surely claims a smile!’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That happiness which is derived from contact of the senses with their objects and which appears like nectar at first but poison at the end is said to be of the nature of passion.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna classifies pleasure that rushes from the senses to their objects as passionate: sweet at the start, bitter at the end.
hinduism.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes enjoyed the nectar of the first eager look and now taste the poison of weeping, which she finds almost laughable.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.38 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a close match for sweet-then-bitter sense pleasure, though the Gita judges it as rajasic while the Kural treats it with rueful humour.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs observes that laughter and sorrow sit close together, and that merriment can end in grief.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural joins the two in the same way: the heroine laughs at eyes whose eager joy has ended in tears.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; it captures the mixture of laughter and grief, though not the self-mockery directed at one’s own eyes.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that it is He who makes [one] laugh and weep.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names laughter and weeping together as conditions that come over human beings in turn.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds both in a single moment: she laughs at the eyes that are weeping.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; it pairs laughter and weeping, but as signs of God’s power rather than as ironic self-reproach.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All things toil to weariness; Man cannot utter it, The eye is not satisfied with seeing, Nor the ear filled with hearing.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth notes that the eye is never sated by looking; it keeps reaching out, and the reaching leads only to weariness.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes, which flew to look and now weep, show the same restless, never-satisfied seeing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); it shares the image of the restless eye, but lacks the Kural’s humour and its love context.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “So long as an evil deed has not ripened, the fool thinks it as sweet as honey. But when the evil deed ripens, the fool comes to grief.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that what tastes sweet at first can ripen into grief, catching the unwary by surprise.
buddhism.tie_back: The eyes’ eager look was honey at first; now it has ripened into weeping, which the heroine finds fit for laughter.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the sweet-then-grief pattern fits, though the verse speaks of evil deeds while the Kural’s look was innocent love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana compares pleasures to the kimpaka fruit, lovely to look at and to taste but deadly afterwards.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine’s eager look was the lovely fruit; the weeping that followed is its bitter after-effect.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi’s diacritics retained); a good image of delight turning to pain, though the Jain text condemns pleasure outright where the Kural only teases.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Psyche, unable to resist, lights a lamp to look at her sleeping husband, Eros; a drop of oil wakes him, he flies away, and she is left weeping for the husband her own eager look has driven off.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Apuleius’s tale, Psyche’s longing to see is the very thing that costs her the beloved and leaves her in tears.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the eyes that rushed to look are the same eyes that must now weep.
greek_mythology.source: Apuleius, Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass) 5.22-24, Cupid and Psyche (paraphrase)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; a close pattern of eager looking followed by tears, though Psyche’s look breaks a prohibition.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hobbes defines laughter as ‘sudden glory’, a passion that arises when we suddenly see some defect or absurdity and feel ourselves above it.
philosophy.explanation: On Hobbes’s account we laugh at folly when we catch it plainly in view.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s laughter at her eyes fits Hobbes’s description: she stands back and sees their folly, even though it is her own.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known definition, not checked word for word this session; it explains the laughter but not the grief beneath it.

kurals.tamil:
பெயலாற்றா நீருலந்த உண்கண் உயலாற்றா
உய்வில்நோய் என்கண் நிறுத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Peyalaatraa neerulandha un-kan uyalaatraa
uyvilnoi en-kan niruththu.
kurals.meaning: Having planted in me a disease I cannot escape or survive, my lovely eyes have wept until their tears are dried up and they can weep no more.
kurals.elementary: Imagine crying so hard and so long that, in the end, no more tears come out. That is how the lady’s eyes feel: they cried and cried, and now they are dry, but the sadness is still there.
kurals.university: Peyal (பெயல்) is literally ‘rain’, so peyal āṟṟā nīr ulanta is ‘the water dried up, no longer able to rain’: the tears themselves are exhausted. Uyal āṟṟā uyvil nōy is a doubled image of fatality, ‘a disease with no escape, which one cannot survive’, and eṉkaṇ niṟuttu ‘having fixed it in me’ (with a pun on kaṇ as both ‘eye’ and ‘in’). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree that the eyes, having caused the incurable love-sickness, are now too dry even to weep. Pope: ‘Those eyes have wept till all the fount of tears is dry, / That brought upon me pain that knows no remedy.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Cloud Messenger, the exiled Yaksha imagines his wife far away, wasted by separation, her eyes swollen and reddened from incessant weeping, lying awake and counting the days until his return.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s poem pictures the separated wife as worn out by tears and sleeplessness.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is the same figure, her eyes exhausted by weeping over an absent husband.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Meghaduta (Uttaramegha), description of the Yaksha’s wife (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; a strong situational match, though no verse number is given.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears. Mine eye is consumed because of grief.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes nights of weeping until his eye is worn out with sorrow.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Mine eye is consumed because of grief’ could serve as a title for the Kural’s chapter, whose eyes have wept themselves dry.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV (verse 7 continues ‘it waxeth old because of all mine enemies’); a close image of eyes worn out by weeping, though its cause is enemies rather than love.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: Jacob grieves so long for his lost son that his eyes are worn white with sorrow.
islam.tie_back: As with the Kural’s heroine, the eyes themselves bear the damage of grief for an absent beloved.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a close match for eyes ruined by longing, though the love is a father’s for his son.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Mine eyes do fail with tears, Mine inwards burn, My liver is poured upon the earth…”
judaism.explanation: The poet of Lamentations weeps until his eyes give out and his whole body is undone by grief.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes likewise ‘fail with tears’ until there are no more to shed.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); the image of eyes failing through tears matches, though the grief is for a ruined city, not an absent husband.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada traces grief to its root in endearment: to hold someone dear is to be exposed to sorrow.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s ‘incurable disease’ is the grief that springs from endearment, and her dried-up eyes are its sign.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it names the root of her grief, but its counsel to be free of endearment runs against the Kural’s celebration of love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The mind of those who always live in unfrequented lodgings, who eat low food, and who subdue their senses, will not be attacked by the foe, Love, who is vanquished as disease is by medicine.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana speaks of love as a disease that can be cured by the medicine of discipline and sense restraint.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural shares the image of love as a disease but denies the cure: for the heroine it is uyvil nōy, a sickness with no escape.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the love-as-disease image is shared, but the Jain text offers a cure where the Kural insists there is none.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Spurned by Narcissus, the nymph Echo hides in the woods and wastes away with grief until her body is gone and only her voice and bones remain.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Echo is consumed by an unreturned love until nothing of her is left but a voice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Echo is worn away by a love-sickness she cannot escape, until even its outward signs are spent.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; it shares the wasting love-sickness but not the image of tears running dry.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius describes love as a sore that, if fed, grows inflamed and becomes chronic, a madness that worsens day by day unless it is broken off early.
philosophy.explanation: For Lucretius, erotic love is a wound that festers rather than heals when one keeps nourishing it.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine calls her love ‘a disease with no escape’; Lucretius explains why it has become so.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it matches the incurable-sickness image but speaks of love in a disparaging Epicurean tone.

kurals.tamil:
படலாற்றா பைதல் உழக்கும் கடலாற்றாக்
காமநோய் செய்தஎன் கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Padalaatraa paidhal uzhakkum kadalaatraak
kaamanoi seydha-en kan.
kurals.meaning: My eyes, which brought on a love-sickness too great for even the sea to hold, now suffer the torment of being unable to sleep.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever been so worried about something that you couldn’t fall asleep, even though you were tired? The lady’s eyes feel that way every night. Her missing-him feeling is so big, bigger than the ocean, that her eyes just can’t close.
kurals.university: The couplet sets two ‘cannot’ compounds against each other: paṭal āṟṟā, ‘unable to lie down (sleep)’, and kaṭal āṟṟā, ‘which the sea cannot hold’, so that the eyes are punished by sleeplessness for a love-sickness larger than the ocean. Paital uḻakkum is ‘are tormented by affliction’. Puliyur Kesikan adds that the eyes suffer ‘through this evil deed’, at night, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar stress that the sickness was caused by the eyes and they now cannot sleep. Pope: ‘The eye that wrought me more than sea could hold of woes, / Is suffering pangs that banish all repose.’ No variant readings were found between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: During the monsoon at Kishkindha, Rama, parted from Sita, cannot rest; the clouds, the rain and the night only sharpen his longing, and he passes the season in sleepless grief.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki depicts Rama’s separation from Sita as a sorrow that keeps him awake through the rainy nights.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama, like the Kural’s heroine, suffers a separation so vast that his eyes find no sleep.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, Rama’s lament in the rainy season (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; strong on sleepless separation, though no sarga number is given and the lover is the husband.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes a distress so deep that his eyes are held open through the night.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes are held waking in the same way, troubled beyond rest.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a close image of sleepless eyes in distress, though the psalm’s trouble is spiritual rather than romantic.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob, rebuked for endlessly remembering Joseph, answers that he lays his unbearable grief before God alone.
islam.tie_back: His grief, like the heroine’s, is too large to be contained or put to rest; it can only be poured out.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; it shares a grief too large to bear, but has no sleeplessness or ocean image and the love is paternal.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Mine eye is poured out, and ceaseth not, Without any intermission,”
judaism.explanation: The poet of Lamentations describes eyes that weep without pause, day and night.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes likewise know no intermission: they cannot even lie down to sleep.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); it matches the unceasing affliction of the eyes, though it speaks of tears rather than sleeplessness and of national grief.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Which is greater, the tears you have shed while transmigrating & wandering this long, long time — crying & weeping from being joined with what is displeasing, being separated from what is pleasing — or the water in the four great oceans?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his monks that the tears shed over separation from the beloved across countless lives exceed all the oceans.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s love-sickness is likewise more than the sea can hold; the Buddha measures the grief of separation by the same ocean.
buddhism.source: Assu Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 15.3 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a striking parallel of separation-grief measured against the ocean, though the sutta’s purpose is to inspire disenchantment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Desiring happiness and being submerged in the ocean of delusion, he forms many plans for warding off misery; and for their sake an impassioned man exerts himself.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana pictures the passionate person as sunk in an ocean of delusion, restlessly scheming to escape misery.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is likewise sunk in a sea-sized love-sickness, too restless to sleep.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the ocean image and restlessness match, but the Jain verse diagnoses delusion rather than describing a lover’s sleeplessness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Eros’s arrow strikes her, Medea lies awake through the night, torn by love for Jason and fear for him, while all the city sleeps around her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius shows Medea’s new love as a torment that will not let her sleep.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s eyes, Medea’s are kept open by a love too great for her to contain.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; a strong match for love-caused sleeplessness, though Medea’s is new love, not separation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza calls human weakness in moderating and restraining the emotions ‘bondage’: a person subject to the emotions is not his own master but is at the mercy of fortune.
philosophy.explanation: On Spinoza’s view, strong passions overpower the mind and leave it unable to rest in its own power.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes are in exactly this bondage: a passion larger than the sea keeps them from sleep.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; a general account of being overpowered by emotion, not specific to love or sleeplessness.

kurals.tamil:
ஓஒ இனிதே எமக்கிந்நோய் செய்தகண்
தாஅம் இதற்பட் டது.
kurals.transliteration:
Ohoh inidhae emakkinnoi seydhakan
thaa-am itharpat tadhu.
kurals.meaning: Oh, how sweet it is! The eyes that gave me this sickness have fallen into the same suffering themselves.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a friend talked you into jumping into a cold pool, and then they slipped and fell in too. You might shiver and giggle, ‘Ha! Now you know how it feels!’ The lady says that to her eyes: they got her into this sadness, and now they are stuck in it too.
kurals.university: The couplet opens with the long exclamation ōo (ஓஒ), an alapeṭai (prosodic lengthening) expressing intense feeling, and closes with the lengthened tāam (தாஅம், ‘they themselves’), both stretched for metre and emphasis. Iṉitē, ‘it is sweet’, is ironic satisfaction: the eyes that ‘made this sickness for us’ (emakku innōy ceyta kaṇ) have ‘fallen into it’ (itaṟpaṭṭatu). Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah specify that the eyes now cannot sleep and weep, while Kalaignar renders the tone as ‘this is a joy to me’. Pope: ‘Oho! how sweet a thing to see! the eye / That wrought this pain, in the same gulf doth lie.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One must deliver himself with the help of his mind, and not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that one’s own faculties can act as one’s friend or as one’s enemy, depending on how they are governed.
hinduism.tie_back: The heroine has discovered her eyes to be her enemy, and takes grim pleasure that the enemy now suffers along with her.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.5 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; the idea of one’s own faculty as enemy fits, but the Gita speaks of the mind (not the eyes) and has no element of satisfaction in its suffering.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that every action returns upon the one who did it.
christianity.tie_back: The eyes sowed this sickness and now reap it, which is why the heroine calls their suffering ‘sweet’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the sowing-and-reaping principle matches the Kural’s logic, though Paul speaks of moral judgment, not a lover’s wry satisfaction.

islam.quote_or_event: “So let them laugh a little and [then] weep much as recompense for what they used to earn.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says that those who delighted briefly will weep at length as the fitting return for their deeds.
islam.tie_back: The Kural sees the same justice in the eyes: they delighted once, and now they weep as their due.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; the laugh-then-weep recompense matches closely, though the verse concerns hypocrites, not a lover’s eyes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein; And he that rolleth a stone, it shall return upon him.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that harm one causes tends to come back upon oneself.
judaism.tie_back: The eyes dug the pit of love-sickness and have fallen into it themselves, which the heroine finds fitting.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close match to the eyes ‘falling into’ the sickness they caused, though Proverbs speaks of malice rather than love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Fools of little wit are enemies unto themselves as they move about doing evil deeds, the fruits of which are bitter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that people who act heedlessly become their own enemies, reaping bitter fruit from their own actions.
buddhism.tie_back: The eyes acted as the heroine’s enemy and now taste the bitter fruit themselves.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the self-as-enemy and bitter-fruit ideas match, though the verse speaks of evil deeds and lacks the Kural’s ironic delight.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Thus the objects of the senses and of the mind cause pain to passionate men, but they never in the least cause any pain to the dispassionate.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that the senses, once passionately attached, bring pain back on the one who indulges them.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes, having been passionate, now feel the pain that passion brings, just as the sutra says.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it supports the idea that the passionate sense suffers, though the Jain point is a call to dispassion, with none of the Kural’s ironic glee.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Oedipus learns the truth, he blinds himself, saying that his eyes shall no longer see the evils he has suffered and done.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Sophocles’ play, Oedipus turns on his own eyes as the guilty organs and punishes them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The heroine likewise treats her eyes as culprits deserving to suffer, though only in a lover’s hyperbole.
greek_mythology.source: Sophocles, Oedipus the King, lines c. 1268-1274 (messenger’s report) (paraphrase)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against a translation this session; it shares the motif of the eyes punished as culprits, but in tragedy, not love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Gorgias, Socrates argues that it is better for a wrongdoer to pay the penalty than to escape it, because just punishment is a cure for the soul.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato’s Socrates, suffering that answers to one’s own wrongdoing is fitting, even good.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s ‘How sweet!’ treats the eyes’ suffering as a just and fitting penalty in exactly this spirit, if with more humour.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known argument, not checked word for word this session; the fittingness of deserved suffering fits, but Plato’s concern is moral wrongdoing, not love.

kurals.tamil:
உழந்துழந் துள்நீர் அறுக விழைந்திழைந்து
வேண்டி அவர்க்கண்ட கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uzhandhuzhan thulneer aruka vizhaindhizhaindhu
vaenti avarkkanda kan.
kurals.meaning: Let the eyes that once gazed on him with melting, eager longing now ache and ache until every tear within them is gone.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes when we feel very sad, we get a little cross with ourselves too. The lady is so sad that she tells her own eyes, ‘You wanted to look at him so much, so now you can cry until you have no tears left!’ It is her way of showing how much she misses him.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on two reduplicated verbs: uḻantu uḻantu, ‘suffering, suffering’, and viḻaintu iḻaintu, ‘desiring, melting with tenderness’, so that the present agony mirrors the past yearning sound for sound. Uḷ nīr aṟuka is an optative, ‘may the water within be cut off’, a mock-curse on the eyes that ‘longed and saw him’ (vēṇṭi avark kaṇṭa kaṇ). Commentators differ on whether the curse is sleeplessness plus tears (Mu. Varadarasanar) or an address directly to the eyes (Kalaignar: ‘O eyes… suffer!’); Puliyur Kesikan reads viḻaintu as part of the past delight. Pope: ‘Aching, aching, let those exhaust their stream, / That melting, melting, that day gazed on him.’ No variants were found between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Held captive in Ravana’s Ashoka grove, Sita, separated from Rama, weeps continually, grows thin and pale, and longs only to see him again.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki’s Sundara Kanda shows Sita wasted by tears and longing for her absent husband.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita’s endless weeping is what the Kural’s heroine wishes on her eyes: tears until they are spent.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, Hanuman finds Sita in the Ashoka grove (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; strong on a wife’s weeping in separation, though Sita does not curse her eyes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!”
christianity.explanation: Jeremiah wishes his eyes could become an unending fountain so that he could weep enough for his grief.
christianity.tie_back: Jeremiah and the Kural both speak to the eyes as wells of tears, though Jeremiah longs for more and the heroine for them to run dry.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; it shares the eyes-as-fountain image, but reverses the wish and concerns national mourning.

islam.quote_or_event: “The eyes are shedding tears and the heart is grieved, and we will not say except what pleases our Lord, O Ibrahim! Indeed we are grieved by your separation.”
islam.explanation: At the death of his infant son, the Prophet weeps openly and names the tears of the eyes as the honest sign of the heart’s grief.
islam.tie_back: In both texts the eyes carry the whole weight of grief at separation from a beloved.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; the tearful eyes of separation-grief match, but the Prophet’s tears are accepted as mercy, with no curse on the eyes.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For these things I weep; Mine eye, mine eye runneth down with water; Because the comforter is far from me…”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations repeats ‘mine eye, mine eye’ as it pours out tears because the one who could comfort is far away.
judaism.tie_back: The doubled ‘mine eye, mine eye’ echoes the Kural’s doubled uḻantu uḻantu, both for eyes weeping because the beloved comforter is absent.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close match in form and feeling, though the absent comforter is God and the grief is national.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ill done is that action of doing which one repents later, and the fruit of which one, weeping, reaps with tears.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada describes an action whose fruit is harvested in tears and regret.
buddhism.tie_back: The eyes’ eager gaze was such an action; the heroine now bids them reap its fruit in tears until none remain.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; reaping with tears matches the Kural’s image, though the verse is about regretted wrongdoing, which love is not.

jainism.quote_or_event: “How can a man who passionately desires ‘colours,’ be happy while he gets, keeps, uses, loses, and misses (those things). Even when he enjoys them, he is never satisfied.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that the eye’s passion brings misery at every stage, including when the thing desired is lost and missed.
jainism.tie_back: The eyes that once ‘longed and melted’ at the sight of him are now in the ‘missing’ stage the sutra describes, and the heroine says they must bear it.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the misery of missing what the eye desired fits, though the Jain verse argues against desire rather than voicing a lover’s grief.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After the loss of all her children, Niobe weeps until she is turned to stone, and even as a rock on a mountain she goes on shedding tears.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Niobe is the image of grief that drains a person of everything but tears.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wishes such unending weeping on her eyes, though she imagines the tears finally running dry.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; strong on endless weeping, but the grief is a mother’s and the tears never stop.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato tells of Leontius, who wanted to look at corpses lying by the wall, struggled against the desire, and finally ran to them with his eyes wide open, crying to his eyes, ‘Look, you wretches, take your fill of the fine sight!’
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the story to show that a part of the soul can be angry with its own desires, even speaking to the eyes as separate culprits.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine curses her eyes in the same way, telling them to suffer their fill for the looking they insisted on.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, with the famous line given without quotation marks because it was not checked word for word this session; a close structural parallel of addressing and cursing one’s own eyes, though Leontius’s desire is morbid rather than loving.

kurals.tamil:
பேணாது பெட்டார் உளர்மன்னோ மற்றவர்க்
காணாது அமைவில கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Paenaadhu pettaar ularmanno matravark
kaanaadhu amaivila kan.
kurals.meaning: There is one who loved me without truly caring for me; and yet my eyes cannot rest without seeing him.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever had a friend who said they liked you but didn’t really act like it, and still you kept looking for them on the playground? The lady feels like that. She knows he isn’t caring for her the way he should, but her eyes still keep searching for him.
kurals.university: Pēṇātu peṭṭār, ‘one who desired (me) without cherishing (me)’, sets peṭṭal (to desire, to love) against pēṇutal (to care for, to tend); uḷar maṉṉō, ‘there is indeed such a one’, carries a sigh of reproach. Avark kāṇātu amaivila kaṇ: ‘without seeing him, the eyes do not settle’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss the first line as ‘loved in word only, not in heart’, and Pope’s prose follows this: ‘He is indeed here who loved me with his lips but not with his heart but mine eyes suffer from not seeing him’, while his verse reads ‘Who loved me once, unloving now doth here remain’. Commentators thus differ on whether the husband is physically near but emotionally absent or simply away; the eyes’ restlessness is the same either way. No variants were found between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda, Radha, hurt that Krishna has gone off to sport with other cowherd women, still cannot stop longing for him and sends her friend to find him.
hinduism.explanation: Radha is wounded by Krishna’s neglect, yet her longing to see him only grows.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Radha knows her beloved has not cared for her as he should, but she cannot rest without seeing him.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, early cantos (Radha’s jealousy and longing) (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s well-known situation, not checked against a translation this session; a strong emotional match, though the Gita Govinda is also read devotionally.

christianity.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song of Songs searches through the night for her beloved and cannot find him.
christianity.tie_back: Her restless seeking is exactly the Kural’s eyes that ‘cannot rest without seeing him’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a close match for restless longing to see the beloved, though the bride does not accuse him of not caring.

islam.quote_or_event: “So We restored him to his mother that she might be content and not grieve and that she would know that the promise of Allah is true.”
islam.explanation: Moses is returned to his mother; the Arabic phrase rendered ‘be content’ is literally that ‘her eye might be cooled’, i.e. at rest, by seeing him.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes have no such rest: only seeing the beloved could ‘cool’ them.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; the link rests on the Arabic idiom of the eye being cooled by seeing a loved one, which the English rendering hides, and the love is maternal.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; But my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved withdraws without explanation, and the woman goes out searching and calling though he does not answer.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the beloved seems not to care, yet she cannot stop seeking to see him.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close match for a beloved who withdraws and a lover who cannot rest without him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada names ‘not seeing the beloved’ as one of the two great sources of pain.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine lives exactly this pain: her eyes cannot rest because they do not see the one they love.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; ‘not to see the beloved is painful’ is almost the Kural’s second line, though the Buddha’s conclusion is to hold nothing dear.

jainism.quote_or_event: Arishtanemi (Neminatha) abandons his bride Rajimati on their wedding day to become a monk; she, though forsaken, sets her heart on following him, and later renounces the world herself.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana tells how Rajimati, left by the groom she loved, still turns her whole life toward him.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Rajimati is loved and yet left uncared for, and still cannot turn her eyes from him.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative, not re-read this session; a genuine story of a forsaken bride, though its resolution is renunciation rather than continued romantic longing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Clytie, abandoned by the Sun god Helios for another, sits on the bare ground for days without food, gazing only at him as he crosses the sky, until she turns into a flower that always faces the sun.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Clytie loves a god who no longer cares for her, yet her eyes never leave him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She is the Kural’s heroine exactly: loved and then neglected, with eyes that cannot rest unless they see him.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; a very close match in both the neglect and the fixed gaze.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that friendships based on pleasure or usefulness are easily dissolved, since when one party no longer finds the other pleasant or useful, he ceases to love.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, love that is not grounded in care for the other person for their own sake does not last.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s husband ‘loved without caring’, the kind of love Aristotle says fades, while her own eyes go on loving.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it explains the husband’s shallow love, but not the eyes’ longing.

kurals.tamil:
வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின்துஞ்சா ஆயிடை
ஆரஞர் உற்றன கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaaraakkaal thunjaa varindhunjaa aayidai
aaranjar utrana kan.
kurals.meaning: When he does not come, my eyes do not sleep; when he comes, they still do not sleep; caught between the two, they suffer unbearable pain.
kurals.elementary: Imagine waiting up for someone you love to come home: you can’t sleep because you’re waiting. Then they come, and you still can’t sleep because you’re so happy, and maybe worried they’ll leave again. The lady’s eyes get no rest either way.
kurals.university: The couplet is a neat antithesis: vārākkāl tuñcā, ‘when he does not come, they do not sleep’, and varin tuñcā, ‘if he comes, they do not sleep’; āyiṭai, ‘between these two’, the eyes uṟṟaṉa ār añar, ‘have met with grievous pain’. Commentators supply the reasons: in absence the eyes watch for his coming, and in presence they fear his departure (Solomon Pappaiah, Puliyur Kesikan: pirivu añci, ‘dreading separation’). Kalaignar generalises it to ‘such suffering can only belong to lovers’ eyes’. Pope: ‘When he comes not, all slumber flies; no sleep when he is there; / Thus every way my eyes have troubles hard to bear.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gopi Gita, the cowherd women tell Krishna that when he goes to the forest by day, even a moment without seeing him feels like an age, and when they do see his face, they curse the creator who made eyelids that blink and interrupt their gaze.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis find no rest either in Krishna’s absence or in his presence: absence is an age, and presence is spoiled by the blink of an eye.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s double bind exactly: the eyes suffer when he does not come and are restless even when he does.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse, not checked against a translation this session; a strikingly close two-sided parallel, though the poem is devotional as well as romantic.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh…”
christianity.explanation: The bride lies down but cannot truly rest, because her heart is always listening for the beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes know the same half-sleep: they cannot let go of watchfulness for him, whether he is absent or near.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a close image of love-kept wakefulness, though it lacks the Kural’s explicit sleeplessness in both absence and presence.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s romance, Majnun, separated from Layla, wanders the desert sleepless with longing, and even when he is allowed near her he cannot be at peace, so consuming is his love.
islam.explanation: Majnun’s love leaves him no rest, whether apart from Layla or close to her.
islam.tie_back: His restlessness on both sides of meeting mirrors the Kural’s eyes that sleep neither when the beloved stays away nor when he comes.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the romance’s general situation, not checked against a translation this session, with no specific passage cited; Islamicate love poetry rather than scripture.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thus I was: in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep fled from mine eyes.”
judaism.explanation: Jacob reminds Laban of his years of service, during which he gave up sleep; he had first served seven years out of love for Rachel.
judaism.tie_back: Jacob’s eyes, like the Kural’s, lost their sleep in a life shaped by love.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); sleep fleeing the eyes matches, but the cause is hard labour, linked only indirectly to love for Rachel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Long is the night to the sleepless; long is the league to the weary. Long is worldly existence to fools who know not the Sublime Truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada begins its chapter on the fool with the image of the sleepless night that never seems to end.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes know that long night, whether her husband is away or present.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the sleepless night is a direct image match, but the verse uses it as a metaphor for samsara, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “How, then, can a man who is devoted to ‘colours,’ ever derive any happiness from anything? He suffers pain at the time of their enjoyment to procure which he had suffered misery.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana says that the one attached to what the eye loves suffers both while seeking it and while enjoying it.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s double bind in Jain terms: pain when he is absent, and pain still when he is present.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a close structural match for suffering both before and during possession, though framed as a warning against attachment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Throughout the Odyssey, Penelope weeps for her absent husband night after night until Athena sheds sleep on her eyelids; and even after Odysseus returns, the couple stay awake through the night of their reunion talking.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s Penelope cannot sleep for grief in Odysseus’s absence, and the night of his return is also a night without sleep.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Her sleepless nights in both absence and presence give the Kural’s double bind a gentler, happier mirror.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of well-known passages, not checked against a translation this session; the absence half is strong, but the reunion night is joyful rather than anxious.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates describes the lover’s soul, parted from the beloved, as maddened and in pain, unable to sleep by night or stay still by day, and running to wherever it hopes to see the beautiful one.
philosophy.explanation: In the Phaedrus, the absence of the beloved leaves the soul sleepless and restless, relieved only by seeing him.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes suffer the same sleeplessness when he is away.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; strong on sleepless longing in absence, though Plato says seeing the beloved brings relief where the Kural says it does not.

kurals.tamil:
மறைபெறல் ஊரார்க்கு அரிதன்றால் எம்போல்
அறைபறை கண்ணார் அகத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Maraiperal ooraarkku aridhandraal empoal
araiparai kannaar agaththu.
kurals.meaning: It is no hard thing for the townsfolk to learn the secret in the hearts of women like me, whose eyes announce it like a beaten drum.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever tried to keep a secret, but your face gave it away? Maybe you were trying not to smile about a surprise, and everyone could tell! The lady says her red, teary eyes are like a loud drum telling the whole town, ‘She misses him!’
kurals.university: Maṟai (மறை) is ‘secret’ and aṟai paṟai (அறைபறை) ‘a drum that is beaten’, the town crier’s drum used for public proclamations; kaṇṇār akattu, ‘in the hearts of those whose eyes (are such drums)’. The couplet closes the chapter by turning from the eyes’ private suffering to their public betrayal: whatever the heroine hides, her tear-stained eyes broadcast it. It also links back to chapter 115 (alar, village gossip). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read the drum as the weeping that reveals the inner state; Pope: ‘It is not hard for all the town the knowledge to obtain, / When eyes, as mine, like beaten tambours, make the mystery plain.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s play, Shakuntala tries to hide her love for King Dushyanta, but her friends Anasuya and Priyamvada read her pallor, sighs and fevered looks and gently draw the secret out of her.
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala’s body and eyes betray the love she is too modest to speak.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she cannot keep her love secret, because her eyes and face announce it to those around her.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against a translation this session; a close match for love betrayed by outward signs, though here before marriage.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest; neither any thing hid, that shall not be known and come abroad.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says that what is hidden will in time come into the open.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine’s secret is ‘made manifest’ by her own eyes, as surely as if it were proclaimed.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the hidden-made-known principle fits, but Jesus speaks of the gospel and judgment, not lovesickness.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of what they have recognized of the truth.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an notes that the tears in people’s eyes openly show what has moved their hearts.
islam.tie_back: In both texts the eyes make the inner state visible to everyone who looks.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; the eyes revealing the heart match, though the tears here are of recognition of truth, not love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance; But by sorrow of heart the spirit is broken.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that the state of the heart shows plainly in the face.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same principle to the eyes: the heart’s sorrow drums itself out through them.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); it matches the heart showing in the face, though it lacks the Kural’s theme of an exposed secret.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Ummadanti Jataka, a king catches one glimpse of the beautiful Ummadanti and is so overcome with longing that he can no longer hide it; his minister sees his condition and learns its cause.
buddhism.explanation: The king’s love-sickness shows itself so plainly that those around him discover what he would keep hidden.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the lover’s secret is broadcast by the state of his body and eyes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the tale’s outline from general knowledge, not checked against a translation this session; the exposed lovesickness fits, though the king’s desire is for another man’s wife and the Jataka condemns it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Anger, pride, deceit, greed; disgust, aversion to self-control and delight in sensual things; mirth, fear, sorrow, carnal desire for women, men, or both; all these manifold passions arise in him who is attached to pleasures…”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana lists the many emotions, sorrow among them, that well up in one who is attached through the senses.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine’s sorrow is such an emotion, and it wells up so strongly that it shows in her eyes for all to see.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (excerpted); a weak, next-best match that explains the arising of sorrow but not its public betrayal by the eyes.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Hippolytus, Phaedra wastes away, refusing food and hiding her love for her stepson, but the chorus and her nurse can see that she is sick at heart, and the nurse finally draws the secret out of her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phaedra’s concealed love is betrayed by her visible decline.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As the Kural says, a secret love cannot stay hidden when the body and eyes announce it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against a translation this session; strong on a hidden love betrayed by outward signs, though Phaedra’s love is illicit and tragic.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld observes that no disguise can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.
philosophy.explanation: The moralist holds that real love inevitably shows itself, whatever one does to conceal it.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s drum-like eyes prove his maxim: her love cannot be hidden from the town.
philosophy.source: François de La Rochefoucauld, Maxims, no. 70 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known maxim, not checked word for word this session; a close match for love’s inability to stay hidden, though it does not single out the eyes.
